items.excerpt: ### Today's top stories Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers. ... Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times. - 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now. Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones. - 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says. Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions. - 🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says.

items.title: Fed Watches Inflation Picture Turn Uglier | Charles Schwab
items.excerpt: Yes, the rise in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) decelerated from 0.6% month over month in September to 0.4% in October. But energy accounted for 58% of September's rise, while in October it accounted for only 15%, making energy a relatively minor factor in the latest reading. Still, October's gain works out to annualized inflation of about 4.3%. Zooming out also reveals a less-than-attractive picture. Over the three months through October, CPI rose an annualized 5.7%, while the wholesale Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand rose an annualized 9%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose at a 3.7% annualized rate during the same period. That's more than double the 1.6% pace it set in the three months through July. Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price data for October is due November 25. PCE is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. But Fed Governor Christopher J. Waller didn't wait for it. Hours before the CPI release on November 10, he said that if October CPI rose 0.3% or ... Waller, who voted to hold rates steady in October, noted particular concern about the breadth of price increases. ... Inflation appears to be spreading. In October, 105 of 177 CPI expenditure categories (59%) rose faster than a 3% annualized rate. That equals the highest level since August 2022, up from 49% in September and 46% in August. In all, 27 categories rose the most in at least a year, including household furnishings and supplies (up 0.7% month over month), motor vehicle insurance (up 0.7%), and club memberships and sports fees (up 1.2%).

items.title: US business activity growth eases further in November, survey shows By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 23 (Reuters) - US business activity growth slowed further in November as high prices held back new orders and capacity constraints restrained output, but overall activity remains resilient, suggesting economic growth is continuing at an above-trend rate, a survey showed on Monday. S&P Global said its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, tracking the manufacturing and services sectors, eased to a four-month low of 54.6 this month from a final reading of 55.9 in October. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. The pace of growth slackened in both manufacturing and the vast services sector, which is responsible for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity. The manufacturing PMI slipped to a three-month low of 54.5 from 54.9 in October, while the services PMI dropped to a four-month low of 54.7 from 56.1 last month. New business in services slid, while new orders in manufacturing were little changed. Input cost pressures eased but remain elevated and suggest inflation overall will stay well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. "Although output growth slowed in November, recent readings have been impressively strong, and the PMI surveys still point to GDP (gross domestic product) rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Growth also remained encouragingly broad-based across both manufacturing and services, with both sectors also still taking on additional staff in numbers that are indicative of a further strong payroll gain during November." The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter thanks to ongoing strength in consumer spending and the frenetic artificial intelligence build-out, and employers added a greater-than-expected 165,000 workers to their payrolls in October. "A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November," Williamson said. "Supply disruptions, widely linked to global shipping delays, also appear to have become more widespread, adding to firms’ concerns about being able to fulfill orders and likely to add further to underlying price pressures in the coming months." The November 12-20 survey period also dovetailed with a sharp selloff in the US stock market, which has been a key pillar supporting consumer spending, on concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. It was not clear from the survey data whether that development contributed to the softening in this month’s PMI readings.

items.title: Key Takeaways from President Williams’s Speech on the Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy
items.excerpt: He then turned to inflation, which he noted is about 3-1/2 percent as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, well above the Fed’s 2 percent target. President Williams attributed this high inflation to an unusual set of shocks driven by higher tariffs on imported goods, supply-chain disruptions and higher energy and commodity prices due to global conflicts, and robust demand associated with the surge in AI-related investments. Of the three, he said that “the effects of tariffs on inflation have largely abated and should not add significantly to inflation in goods prices in the future.” At the same time, there is little evidence of significant spillovers into broader and more persistent inflation, and other indicators are encouraging, he said. ... “Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can—and must—ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations,” he said. “Importantly, monetary policy works with a lag of one to two years for its maximal effect on the economy. ... In terms of his economic outlook, President Williams said he expects: - Real GDP growth to increase about 2-3/4 percent this year and to be near that pace next year. - Unemployment to edge down to about 4 percent over the next year. - Overall inflation to come in at about 3-1/2 percent this year, and for inflation to slow to just above 2 percent next year, then reach the FOMC’s longer-run inflation goal of 2 percent in 2028.

items.excerpt: ## Legal fight over 20,000 California ballots ends as appeals court approves DOJ dismissal A federal appeals court today approved the Justice Department’s bid to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots until officials could verify the immigration statuses of recipients it alleged were noncitizens. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decision marked the official end to a flurry of litigation in California immediately preceding the competitive and high-stakes November midterms. Federal prosecutors who brought the lawsuit previously said that their efforts would become moot after Election Day, since local officials would no longer be able to prevent ballots from being counted. The contested ballots were at the heart of a protracted legal battle between the Trump administration and California over the eligibility of voters in the heavily Democratic state, and came amid broader federal scrutiny of local elections nationally.

items.title: Daily Music Headlines November 23, 2026 - Daily Music Headlines | Acast
items.excerpt: Monday, November 23, 2026 Miley Cyrus married drummer and collaborator Maxx Morando Saturday in a private Palm Springs ceremony officiated by Flaming Lips frontman Wayne Coyne. Cyrus and Morando have been together since 2021. Coyne and Cyrus have collaborated for more than a decade, including on Miley Cyrus and Her Dead Petz and “We A Family.” Cyrus released Bass Persuades in September, while the Flaming Lips’ The Teardrop Throbs arrives in January on Third Man Records. Stone Sour have released “Full of Empty,” a previously unreleased track from the 15th anniversary deluxe edition of Audio Secrecy. Corey Taylor revisited an instrumental left off the 2010 album, added lyrics and vocals, and brought in Jim Root and Josh Rand for new guitar parts. The band has been on hiatus since 2020. ... Blondie have released “Come Back Home,” featuring Lucius, the second single from High Noon, due February 26 on BMG. It’s the band’s final album with longtime drummer Clem Burke, who died last year. Lucius’ Jess Wolfe and Holly Laessig wrote the melancholic song about touring and distance. Bradford Cox surprise-released Thanatos, the first Atlas Sound album in 15 years. Recorded alone in his Atlanta attic on a portable 8-track, the 10-song album is out digitally through 4AD, with vinyl planned for next year. It completes the trilogy begun with Logos and Parallax. Cox has upcoming appearances at Big Ears, Kilby Block Party and Primavera Sound. The Offspring announced Just the Punk Stuff, a live album recorded September 18 at Sea.Hear.Now in Asbury Park. The 13-song collection arrives January 29, selected by two superfans from the band’s 23-song set. A video for “Jennifer Lost the War” is out now, and the band will support Fall Out Boy on their Summer 2027 tour. Muse guitarist Matt Bellamy wants to build AI into guitars, allowing players to prompt instruments for specific sounds. He says the technology isn’t quite ready, but Muse already uses AI to operate the sound desk on some tour songs and deliver the opening speech to “Psycho.” Bellamy expects live music with real musicians to keep growing.
